sources.title: Corrigibility
sources.authors: Nate Soares; Benja Fallenstein; Eliezer Yudkowsky; Stuart Armstrong

inspection.read: Introduction, section 2 shutdown desiderata and section 5 discussion, PDF pp.1–3 and 8–9.
inspection.limit: Not a reproduction of all utility calculations; absence of a reserve loop in these passages is not a claim about all corrigibility literature.

sources.prior_proposition: Corrigibility includes cooperating with correction, not inducing or preventing shutdown, and preserving shutdown behavior in successors. The paper explicitly treats defining safe shutdown as difficult beyond its simplified assumptions.

comparison.variables: Utility, actions, shutdown channel versus institutional reserve stocks.
comparison.causal_structure: Agent incentive model, not candidate's external provisioning feedback.
comparison.beneficiary: Creators versus residents and substitute workers.
comparison.outcome: Cooperative shutdown versus executable collective veto.
comparison.timescale: Decision episodes and successors versus budget cycles.
comparison.prediction: Compliance alone cannot establish candidate's resource adequacy.
comparison.intervention: Utility/incentive engineering versus funding and reserve institutions.

sources.title: Nobody Ever Gets Credit for Fixing Problems That Never Happened: Creating and Sustaining Process Improvement
sources.authors: Nelson P. Repenning; John D. Sterman

inspection.read: Printed pp.66–74 and 80–83: stock/flow, Reinvestment, Shortcuts, reward feedback and maintenance case passages.
inspection.limit: Not every field case or supporting simulation replicated; 2002 successor paper discovered but not counted as inspected.

sources.prior_proposition: Capability is an investment-and-decay stock. Short-run performance gains can drain maintenance and training; delayed decline reinforces reduced improvement. Reinvested savings can reverse the same loop into sustained capability growth.

comparison.variables: Very close capability, decay, funding, savings and observed performance.
comparison.causal_structure: Close endogenous investment/decay loop; veto-use proxy differs.
comparison.beneficiary: Organizations and workers versus refusal-capacity commons.
comparison.outcome: Capability trap versus inability to execute joint refusals.
comparison.timescale: Both delayed investment and repeated budget decisions.
comparison.prediction: Success-conditioned capability erosion and reinvestment reversal already follow.
comparison.intervention: Same reinvestment/protected maintenance; adds rights-specific joint frontier.

records.name: Immediate stopping versus recognized collective release
records.strongest_version: All local safety stops are immediately honored. If a common event compresses residual-disposition arrivals that previously would be dispersed, a finite common settlement pool delays counterpart release. If that delay independently creates additional legitimate reconciliation work, rather than merely leaving a finite original compensation list unfinished, the resulting return can prolong aggregate release after agent execution has ceased.
known: Burst intake exhausting fixed service capacity is inherited queue behavior.
Delay/retry amplification and overload sustained after trigger removal are close whole-composition predecessors in metastable-failure research.
Local cancellation differing from semantic compensation and global restoration is explicitly inherited from transaction systems.
Systemic unwind degrading the capacity supporting further unwind is inherited in liquidity-spiral models, with different financial state variables.
The T07 recurrence and its unstable boundary are elementary stipulated stock/flow mathematics; no novel formal result is claimed.
records.new_residue: Only a domain-specific test remains: whether immediately stopped agent mandates induce compressed disposition and genuinely new counterparty obligations that sustain release delay. The general burst–delay–additional-work mechanism and compensation distinction are already close matches; a new mechanism or prediction has not been established.

sources.title: Metastable Failures in Distributed Systems
sources.authors: Nathan Bronson; Abutalib Aghayev; Aleksey Charapko; Timothy Zhu

inspection.read: Sections 1–3, PDF pp.1–4, especially 2.1 retries, 2.3 error handling and adaptive policies/prioritization.
inspection.limit: Simplified operating examples; no reproduction of production incidents or complete literature coverage.

sources.prior_proposition: A transient overload can trigger latency-dependent retries or expensive error handling that sustains resource exhaustion after the trigger ends; reserve headroom, retry budgets and adapted priorities can break the feedback.

comparison.variables: Close arrivals, latency, amplified work, capacity and backlog.
comparison.causal_structure: Close complete congestion–delay–extra-work return.
comparison.beneficiary: Service users versus stopped-mandate counterparties and principals.
comparison.outcome: Persistent overload versus delayed recognized release.
comparison.timescale: Queue episodes in both; application duration can differ.
comparison.prediction: Removing trigger alone may not restore service; already predicted.
comparison.intervention: Same burst capacity, amplification budget and independent queue priorities.

sources.title: Metastable Failures in the Wild
sources.authors: Lexiang Huang; Matthew Magnusson; Abishek Bangalore Muralikrishna; Salman Estyak; Rebecca Isaacs; Abutalib Aghayev; Timothy Zhu; Aleksey Charapko

inspection.read: Sections 3.3–3.5, Figure 1, definitions and theorem statements, PDF pp.6–9; primary conference metadata.
inspection.limit: Proof appendices and all 22 incident reconstructions not inspected. Bounded amplification of organic load differs from T07's unbounded backlog-proportional work.

sources.prior_proposition: Load spikes and capacity decreases can trigger workload amplification or capacity degradation. Delayed retries increase request count or cost; headroom and bounded amplification govern whether overload persists after trigger removal.

comparison.variables: Close load, capacity, amplification, trigger duration and headroom.
comparison.causal_structure: Close whole return; not identical zero-input stock recurrence.
comparison.beneficiary: Distributed-service users versus institutional obligation holders.
comparison.outcome: Metastable overload versus collective disposition delay.
comparison.timescale: Both post-trigger recovery horizons.
comparison.prediction: Follow-on amplification defeating trigger removal is already predicted.
comparison.intervention: Same remove amplification/add headroom; obligation legitimacy requires care.

sources.title: The Transaction Concept: Virtues and Limitations

inspection.read: Introduction; general model; Nested Transactions and Long-Lived Transactions, printed pp.144–145 and 152–153, extracted lines 40–148 and 897–1065.
inspection.limit: Historical transaction model, not legal advice or a claim about current contract law; no reconstruction of cited deadlock formulas.

sources.prior_proposition: A canceled travel plan cannot unilaterally abort already completed airline or hotel transactions; compensation must reverse their semantics. Long-lived interleaved transactions make concurrency, restoration and recovery difficult.

comparison.variables: Same actor cancellation, external commitments, interleaving and compensation.

comparison.outcome: Compensated cancellation versus recognized release.
comparison.timescale: Long-lived transactions and settlement horizons closely overlap.

sources.title: Sagas

inspection.read: Princeton manuscript dated January 7, 1987; PDF pp.2–5 (abstract and complete opening reservation/compensation passages) using OCR.
inspection.limit: Scanned pages have no extractable text; OCR equations were not treated as verified formal results. Remaining implementation and cost sections not inspected.

sources.prior_proposition: Long transactions can release resources through interleaved subtransactions, but partial execution needs semantic compensation. Compensation cancels the relevant effect without necessarily restoring the prior global database state.

comparison.variables: Same reservations, interleaving, release and compensating transactions.
comparison.causal_structure: Compensation structure matches; endogenous new-work return not established.
comparison.beneficiary: Transaction users and other transactions versus human counterparties.
comparison.outcome: Semantic amendment versus complete recognized release.
comparison.timescale: Long transaction and compensation episodes overlap.
comparison.prediction: Local resource release differs from global restoration; already predicted.
comparison.intervention: Same semantic compensation rather than rewind; no forced deletion.

sources.title: Market Liquidity and Funding Liquidity
sources.authors: Markus K. Brunnermeier; Lasse Heje Pedersen

inspection.read: Author-hosted accepted advance-access paper, Figure 2/introduction and section surrounding Proposition 5, PDF pp.4–5 and 18–19; published 2009 identity verified.
inspection.limit: No full proof or empirical reconstruction; no cash collateral or prices assumed in M105.

sources.prior_proposition: Funding constraints and market illiquidity reinforce one another through margin and loss spirals; forced position reductions can worsen liquidity and further constrain the capacity supporting orderly trade.

comparison.variables: Unwind demand/shared capacity overlap; prices and margins differ.
comparison.causal_structure: Analogous unwind–capacity feedback, not an identical settlement queue.
comparison.beneficiary: Traders/market participants versus obligation holders.
comparison.outcome: Liquidity collapse versus recognized-release delay.
comparison.timescale: Trading episodes versus settlement-work horizons.
comparison.prediction: Joint unwind need not share individual capacity assumptions.
comparison.intervention: Liquidity provision versus disposition reserve; no automatic policy transfer.
